1.a4.name: Ware Opening
1.a4.background: Named after Preston Ware, the American player who favoured uncommon openings and played them in tournaments around 1880. Carlsen opened with it against Radjabov at the 2012 World Blitz Championship as a joke, and won.

1.a4 e5.strategy: The principal answer: Black takes space in the centre, which is exactly what 1.a4 ignores, and opens the diagonal for the f8-bishop. The bishop also stands guard over a3, so White's plan of swinging the rook out along the third rank is shut down for now. Black gets the easier game.

1.a4 b6.strategy: A sound but modest reply: Black prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop on the long diagonal and leaves the centre pawns for later. It is perfectly playable, yet it hands White a free hand to occupy the centre, which 1.a4 has not yet done.

1.a4 a5.name: Ware Opening: Symmetric Variation
1.a4 a5.background: With the black pieces, Ware himself played 1...a5.
1.a4 a5.strategy: Mirrors White and stops the a-pawn from advancing, which removes any use White might find for the pawn on the edge. It is harmless but passive: Black fails to take the centre that White has left open, and the game starts level in a very quiet form.

1.a4 b5.strategy: Gives a pawn away: the b5 pawn is attacked by the a-pawn and not defended, so White simply takes it. Black's only return is an open diagonal for the queen's bishop, which is not enough for a pawn.

1.a4 b5 2.axb5.strategy: Takes the free pawn, and Black has no way to win it back at once. White stays a pawn up and opens the a-file for the rook, while the pawn on b5 cramps the queenside; Black's compensation is limited to quick development.

1.a4 b5 2.d4.strategy: Ignores the offered pawn and takes the centre. If Black captures on a4, the rook recaptures and stands on the half-open a-file, but the extra pawn that taking on b5 wins is gone, so White settles for an equal game.

1.a4 b5 2.b3.strategy: Meets the gambit by letting Black take on a4 and recapturing with the b-pawn, which opens the b-file and prepares to fianchetto the c1-bishop. Sound and level, but it gives back the pawn that White could simply keep.

1.a4 b5 2.axb5 Bb7.name: Ware Opening: Wing Gambit
1.a4 b5 2.axb5 Bb7.strategy: The idea behind the gambit: the bishop fianchettoes at once onto the long diagonal, from where it eyes the kingside and the centre. Black is still a pawn down and has only quick development to show for it, but this is the most useful way to spend the tempo.

1.a4 b5 2.axb5 a6.strategy: Challenges the pawn on b5 at once. If White takes on a6, Black recaptures with a piece and gets quick development and play against White's queenside, though White is still a pawn up.

1.a4 b5 2.axb5 c6.strategy: Contests the pawn from the other side and frees the queen's diagonal. White can take again on c6, so Black is still behind in material and has spent time on pawn moves for little more than a slightly freer game.

1.a4 b6 2.d4.strategy: White claims the centre at once, as the opening itself has not, and gives the c1-bishop its diagonal. Black's planned fianchetto on the long diagonal finds the centre already held by a solid pawn that White can support with natural development. It is the most sensible way to use the tempo.

1.a4 b6 2.e4.strategy: Claims the centre with the e-pawn at once and opens lines for the king's bishop and the queen. The bishop on b7 hits the pawn immediately, but a developing move defends it, and White keeps the broad centre that the fianchetto was meant to challenge.

1.a4 b6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops towards the centre and controls e5 and d4 without committing the central pawns. It keeps every set-up open and makes use of the tempo, since the early a-pawn move has not gained space anywhere that matters.

1.a4 b6 2.d4 d5.strategy: Black answers the centre pawn with a pawn of its own and keeps the position balanced and closed. It blocks the d-file, but the pawn is only guarded by the queen and so ties it down.

1.a4 b6 2.d4 Bb7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop controls the long diagonal and presses on the centre from a distance, and on the g2 pawn behind it. Black has not yet decided how to meet the d4 pawn and keeps both central pawn moves available.

1.a4 b6 2.d4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and watches e4, so White cannot build a broad centre unchallenged. Combined with the fianchetto it controls the centre from a distance instead of occupying it, a flexible and sound way to play against the d4 pawn.

1.a4 b6 2.d4 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and prepares a solid centre, while the c8-bishop is still free to fianchetto. The set-up is sound and flexible, if a little slower than meeting the centre with a knight.

1.a4 b6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops with a direct attack on d5, so Black must keep the pawn guarded. It pressures the centre while keeping the structure flexible, and tests whether Black will defend with a piece or give ground.

1.a4 b6 2.d4 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it guards d4 and keeps an eye on e5, and leaves the c- and e-pawns free to decide how to meet the d5 pawn. There is no need to rush: a patient build-up leaves Black to show what the b6 set-up is for.

1.a4 b6 2.d4 d5 3.c4.strategy: Challenges the d5 pawn from the flank. If Black takes, the pawn is soon won back, since the a4 pawn stops ...b5 from holding it; if Black holds with ...e6, the game is a solid queen's pawn structure in which White's pieces are the more active.

1.a4 b6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nd7.name: Ware Opening: Cologne Gambit
1.a4 b6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nd7.strategy: Develops a knight but blocks the queen's defence of d5, so 4.Nxd5 wins a pawn. Black hopes for development in return, with the bishop heading for the long diagonal and the knight's way to f6 still open, but is simply a pawn down.

1.a4 b6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Answers the attack on d5 by developing a second defender, so the pawn holds without the queen being tied to it. Black stays solid and flexible, with the fianchetto bishop still to come, and meets White's centre without weakening anything.

1.a4 b6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb7.strategy: Adds a second guard to d5 along the long diagonal, so Nxd5 would simply lose the knight to the bishop. Black completes the fianchetto, but the kingside pieces are still undeveloped.

1.a4 b6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 with a pawn, taking the load off the queen, and opens the f8-bishop. Solid, though a little passive: Black accepts a cramped but sound position and leaves White the initiative in the centre.

1.a4 e5 2.h4.name: Ware Opening: Crab Variation
1.a4 e5 2.h4.strategy: A second rim-pawn move that does nothing for development or the centre. The pawn is guarded by the rook and so stops the black queen using h4, but that is all it gains, and White has spent two moves on the edge while Black builds a centre.

1.a4 e5 2.a5.strategy: Pushes the edge pawn a second time while Black builds the centre. The pawn gains some space on the wing, but it has no further job there, and White falls behind in development and control of the middle.

1.a4 e5 2.Ra3.name: Ware Opening: Meadow Hay Trap
1.a4 e5 2.Ra3.strategy: Walks into a simple loss: 2...Bxa3 wins the exchange, since the f8-bishop already looks down the diagonal to a3. White recaptures with the b-pawn, wrecking the queenside structure, or with the knight, leaving it on the edge, and is a clear exchange down.

1.a4 e5 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre at once and opens lines for the king's bishop and the queen. Black has an extra tempo for development, as the a-pawn move has done little, but the centre is shared and White can simply develop.

1.a4 e5 2.d4.strategy: Challenges the black centre pawn immediately. If Black takes, the queen recaptures but is hit by ...Nc6 and has to move again, so White regains the pawn at the cost of a tempo and stands slightly passively.

1.a4 e5 2.a5 d5.strategy: Black ignores the advanced a-pawn and takes the full centre with a second pawn. The pawn on a5 has no target and no further job, so White has spent two moves on the wing while Black stands better in the middle.

1.a4 e5 2.a5 a6.strategy: Fixes the advanced pawn on a5, so that it can never push on to a6, and keeps the wing closed. It is safe, but it spends a tempo on a move that was not needed, and Black still has to take the centre afterwards.

1.a4 e5 2.a5 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece towards the centre and controls e4 and d5, leaving the pawn decisions for later. The a5 pawn is still no danger, so Black can simply carry on developing while White has spent two moves on the wing.

1.a4 e5 2.a5 d5 3.e3.strategy: Prepares d4 with a pawn behind it, so the break comes without the queen being hit by ...Nc6, and opens the f1-bishop and the queen. It lets Black keep the broad centre for now, but it is the sound base from which to undermine it.

1.a4 e5 2.a5 d5 3.d4.strategy: Challenges the black centre at once. If Black takes, the queen recaptures and is hit by ...Nc6, so White loses time; if Black pushes ...e4, the centre locks and White must undermine the chain from the side. Good, direct play, but it costs more than preparing the break with e3.

1.a4 e5 2.a5 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and attacks e5, but ...e4 drives it away with a tempo, and ...c5 may chase it again if it goes to d4. Black gains space on the way, so this is playable but gives Black the easier game.

1.a4 e5 2.a5 d5 3.e3 f5.strategy: Black builds a broad pawn centre and gains space for an advance in the middle. The cost is a looser king: the diagonal from e8 to h5 opens, and the e6 square is weak.

1.a4 e5 2.a5 d5 3.e3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to a natural square, where it supports e4 and d5 without loosening the king's diagonal. Black already has the bigger share of the centre and White's wing pawn moves have bought nothing, so quiet development is all that is needed.

1.a4 e5 2.a5 d5 3.e3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece with pressure on d4 and on the a5 pawn, which only the rook protects. It supports the advance of the centre pawns and is solid, though the knight blocks the c-pawn.

1.a4 e5 2.a5 d5 3.e3 f5 4.a6.name: Ware Opening: Ware Gambit
1.a4 e5 2.a5 d5 3.e3 f5 4.a6.strategy: A pawn sacrifice that opens the a-file. Black wins the pawn, best with the knight, but White gets quick development and a bishop on f1 aimed at a6, and a recapture with the b-pawn would leave Black's pawns weak. Playable, but White has to make the activity pay.

1.a4 e5 2.a5 d5 3.e3 f5 4.d4.strategy: Challenges the black pawn centre before it advances further. If Black locks the centre with ...e4, White undermines the chain from the side and Black's open king diagonal from e8 to h5 stays a target.

1.a4 e5 2.a5 d5 3.e3 f5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight with pressure on d5, but Black simply holds d5 with ...c6, and the knight takes c3 away from the c-pawn, so the pressure achieves little. Sound, yet it gives White less than striking at once in the centre.
